title: Electric Potential
short_intro: Electric potential at a point in an electric field is defined as the work done per unit positive test charge in bringing it from infinity to that point without acceleration. It is a scalar quantity governing the electrostatic potential energy of charges.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of electric potential, potential due to a point charge, superposition principle, relation between electric field and potential, equipotential surfaces, and potential energy of a system of point charges.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Potential due to continuous charge distributions (ring, disc, spherical shell, solid sphere), dipole potential at any general point, multipole expansion, Poisson's and Laplace's equations, and electrostatic potential energy of continuous charge configurations.

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Scalar Nature
bullets: Electric potential V at a point is given by V = W/q<sub>0</sub>, where W is the work done by an external agent against electrostatic forces in bringing a positive test charge q<sub>0</sub> from infinity.
It is a scalar quantity, meaning potentials due to multiple charges add algebraically.
The SI unit of electric potential is Joule per Coulomb (J/C) or Volt (V).

concept_notes.heading: Relation between Electric Field and Potential
bullets: The electric field is the negative gradient of the electric potential: E = -dV/dr.
In three dimensions, E = -((partial V/partial x)hat{i} + (partial V/partial y)hat{j} + (partial V/partial z)hat{k}).
Electric field lines point in the direction of decreasing electric potential.

concept_notes.heading: Equipotential Surfaces
bullets: An equipotential surface is a surface with a constant value of electric potential at all points on it.
The electric field vector is always normal (perpendicular) to the equipotential surface at every point.
No work is done in moving a test charge between two points on the same equipotential surface.

concept_notes.heading: Electrostatic Potential Energy
bullets: The potential energy U of a system of charges is the total work done in assembling the charges from infinity to their current configuration.
For a two-point charge system, U = (1/4piepsilon<sub>0</sub>) * (q<sub>1</sub>q<sub>2</sub> / r).
Potential energy is associated with conservative forces and satisfies Delta U = -W_{electric} = qDelta V.

derivations.title: Potential due to a Point Charge
derivations.conditions: Static point charge q placed at the origin in vacuum
steps: Consider a test charge q<sub>0</sub> at a distance r from a source charge q.
The electrostatic force on the test charge at distance x is F = (1/4piepsilon<sub>0</sub>) * (qq<sub>0</sub> / x<sup>2</sup>) along the radial direction.
The work done by the electric field in moving the test charge from r to infinity is W = int_{r}^{infty} F dx.

derivations.title: Potential due to an Electric Dipole at a General Point
derivations.conditions: Short electric dipole of dipole moment p, distance r >> length of dipole
steps: Let r be the position vector of the observation point making an angle 	heta with the dipole axis.
The potential due to charges +q and -q at distances r<sub>1</sub> and r<sub>2</sub> is V =  rac{q}{4piepsilon_0} ( rac{1}{r_1} -  rac{1}{r_2}).
Using approximations r_1 approx r - (d/2)cos	heta and r_2 approx r + (d/2)cos	heta, substitute into the potential expression.
Simplifying the algebraic difference gives V =  rac{pcos	heta}{4piepsilon_0 r^2}.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Potential (V) and Electric Field (E) versus Distance (r) for a Point Charge
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Plot V vs r as a rectangular hyperbola decreasing as 1/r, and E vs r decreasing more steeply as 1/r<sup>2</sup> on the same axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that potential falls off slower with distance than electric field intensity.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked conceptual questions comparing the spatial decay rates of E and V.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Equipotential Surfaces for a Point Charge
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Concentric spherical shells centered on the charge, with radial electric field lines intersecting them orthogonally.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that potential is constant on the spherical surfaces and field lines are perpendicular to them.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Visual identification of equipotential patterns for point charges and uniform fields.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Potential inside and outside a Uniformly Charged Conducting Sphere
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A flat horizontal line inside (V = constant = Q/4piepsilon<sub>0</sub>R) and a 1/r decay curve outside the radius R.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Reflects the zero electric field inside a conductor, implying constant potential throughout the interior volume.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical and conceptual problems on distribution of potential in conductors.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the electric potential at a distance of 9 cm from a point charge of 2 mu C.
solution_steps: Identify given values: q = 2 mu C = 2 	imes 10^{-6} C, r = 9 cm = 0.09 m.
Recall formula: V =  rac{1}{4piepsilon_0}  rac{q}{r} where 1/(4piepsilon<sub>0</sub>) = 9 	imes 10^9 N m<sup>2</sup>/C<sup>2</sup>.
Substitute values: V = (9 	imes 10^9 	imes 2 	imes 10^{-6}) / 0.09.
Calculate result: V = (18 	imes 10^3) / 0.09 = 2 	imes 10^5 V.

solved_numericals.question: Two point charges q<sub>1</sub> = +1 mu C and q<sub>2</sub> = -2 mu C are placed at vertices (0, 0, 3) m and (0, 0, -3) m respectively. Find the electrostatic potential at point (4, 0, 0) m.
solution_steps: Determine distance from q<sub>1</sub> (0,0,3) to (4,0,0): r<sub>1</sub> = sqrt{(4-0)^2 + (0-0)^2 + (0-3)^2} = sqrt{16 + 9} = 5 m.
Determine distance from q<sub>2</sub> (0,0,-3) to (4,0,0): r<sub>2</sub> = sqrt{(4-0)^2 + (0-0)^2 + (0-(-3))^2} = sqrt{16 + 9} = 5 m.
Use superposition principle: V =  rac{1}{4piepsilon_0} ( rac{q_1}{r_1} +  rac{q_2}{r_2}).
Substitute values: V = (9 	imes 10^9) 	imes ( rac{1 	imes 10^{-6}}{5} +  rac{-2 	imes 10^{-6}}{5}).
Calculate result: V = (9 	imes 10^9) 	imes ( rac{-1 	imes 10^{-6}}{5}) = -1800 V.

solved_numericals.question: How much work is done in moving a charge of 2 C from a point where potential is 10 V to another point where potential is 30 V?
solution_steps: Identify given values: q = 2 C, V<sub>initial</sub> = 10 V, V<sub>final</sub> = 30 V.
Use work-potential relation: W = q(V<sub>final</sub> - V<sub>initial</sub>).

assumptions_and_limitations: Reference point for zero electric potential is assumed to be at infinity for localized charge distributions.
Electrostatic potential assumes static charges; time-varying magnetic fields introduce induced non-conservative electric fields where scalar potential alone is insufficient.

common_misconceptions.wrong: If the electric field at a point is zero, the electric potential must also be zero.
common_misconceptions.correct: Electric potential can be non-zero even when the electric field is zero (e.g., inside a charged hollow conducting sphere).
common_misconceptions.why: Electric field is the negative spatial derivative of potential, so a constant non-zero potential yields a zero derivative (field).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Work done in moving a charge between two points depends on the path taken.
common_misconceptions.correct: Work done by an electrostatic field is completely independent of the path taken.
common_misconceptions.why: Electrostatic force is conservative, meaning work depends only on the initial and final positions.

quick_revision: Electric potential is a scalar quantity obeying the principle of linear superposition.
Electric Potential of Point Charge: V = \frac{1}{4piepsilon_0} \frac{q}{r}
